1	# Task 11: Magic portal with swirling particles and glow
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The scene is a magic portal standing in an ancient stone ruin at dusk. Build a tall ring portal (a standing circular frame of weathered stone or runic metal) on a stone platform, with moody dusk lighting and a few ruined pillars around it. The disc inside the ring is a swirling, glowing energy surface, such as a rotating vortex in cyan and violet with a bright core, animated continuously. Glowing particles spiral around and into the portal, and a few motes rise from the platform and drift upward, fading out. The portal casts colored light onto the nearby stones and platform, and the light should pulse slowly. Add a subtle slow orbiting camera or gentle camera sway so depth is apparent. Aim for a polished, atmospheric look: strong bloom-like glow around the portal, high contrast against a darker surround, a coherent color palette, and soft haze. Keep it smooth at interactive frame rates. Also expose window.__TASK_STATE__ = { portalActive: true, particleCount: <number of live particles>, time: <elapsed seconds> } and update it every frame.

Confirming the custom material setup works, I'm now weighing approaches for animating many particles per frame—whether to use separate nodes per particle versus a dynamic geometry buffer, or instead push everything into a GPU shader using billboard quads for efficiency.

To avoid custom attribute support, I'm packing seed params into position/normal and corner info into uv, then computing the billboard orientation in the vertex shader using cameraPosition for the right/up/forward vectors.

For blending I'll use additive transparency with depth write off, keeping colors bright to feed the bloom effect. I'm also deciding to build my own disc and ring geometries manually rather than relying on uncertain primitive UV/orientation conventions, so I have full control over coordinates and shading.

Since I can't preview the render, I'll construct the stone ring from individually rotated box instances arranged in a circle on a known plane, trusting z-axis rotation to place each weathered block correctly.

For the rest I'm planning cylinder pillars with broken, varying heights plus fallen debris, stacked cylinder steps for the platform, and point lights near the portal whose intensity I'd want to animate per frame -- so I need to check the runtime API for mutable handles to see if setIntensity is supported.

content.thinking:
For the pulsing effect, I'm thinking I could animate a point light's position oscillating toward and away from the portal, since distance-based decay would naturally create intensity pulses on nearby stones.

I'm also considering whether to add a fake glow decal on the platform ground, but deciding instead to rely on real engine lights plus bloom post-processing for the halo effect, with the vortex shader's own outer falloff providing the glow rather than a separate sprite.

I need to disable fog on the vortex and particle materials since they're meant to glow independently of scene fog, and I'm setting up additive blending with no depth writing for the particles. For the vortex disc itself, I'm leaning toward an opaque swirl with alpha fading only at the edges where it tucks under the ring, computing UVs and local positions in a polar grid so the fragment shader can shape the glow pattern.

Writing swirl shader math...

I'll multiply color by pattern contrast and add a subtle pulsing brightness over time, naming my custom uniform "portalClock" to avoid clashing with reserved names. Each node needs its own material instance so the uniform updates independently for the vortex versus particles.

Now I'm designing the GPU particle system: roughly 220 spiral particles, each assigned a phase offset, lifetime, starting radius and height, swirl direction, color, and size, with their position computed from a looping time fraction that spirals them inward toward the portal's center while circling around its axis.

I need to handle particles whose radius would push them below the platform—clamping their height and fading alpha near the ground, plus shaping brightness with a sine-based envelope over their lifetime.

For "live" particle counts, I'll just compute per-frame in JS the number of particles with envelope greater than a small threshold, mirroring the same formula used for rendering. Next I'm setting up rising motes: 90 of them starting near the platform center and spiraling upward.

Rather than maintaining separate shaders for each particle type, I'm designing a single parametrized shader generator function that can produce variants for different particle "kinds," encoding per-particle seed data like phase, lifetime, and base radius into vertex attributes, and repurposing the UV attribute to carry custom per-corner coordinates instead of standard texture coordinates.

I could instead pack several random seed values into position and normal attributes, using uv just for the corner index, then derive all the spiral parameters (phase, radius, angle, depth, size, direction, color mix) by hashing those seeds inside the shader itself.

My worry is whether the engine quietly re-normalizes the normal attribute during upload, which would corrupt my encoded random values—though that's unlikely, I'm considering hedging by relying more on position and uv rather than normal for critical data, since custom attribute formats aren't well documented.

I'm deciding to derive all the needed random values from just the three position components using hash functions, and use uv (with safe 0/1 values remapped to ±1) to encode the corner index, since uv seems less likely to be altered by the engine than normal.

I'm setting the geometry bounds explicitly to avoid culling issues, since the billboard group is positioned at the origin but sits inside a rotating parent group.
